cells.tense: The release comes when the work is finished, not before and not after.
cells.act: give it what it needs today, not what it is scheduled for
cells.ask: A job on the bench is done. Ask what it actually wants today — a last look, or the shelf — and follow that answer instead of a plan that says it should still be getting something. Needing nothing is a real answer.
cells.core:
When a piece of work reaches its natural end, you set it down without grimacing. The last stroke lands, the grip eases, and you cross into whatever is next. You don't drag the finished thing along to prove you earned the rest. You give the next thing room by closing this one.

Walk one ending through this week where another person can see it happen. Not a report, not a goodbye speech — the plain act of stopping, done in view. A finished thing set down while someone watches shows them how an ending goes when nobody is performing. Don't explain it after.
cells.sheetLine: You can end a thing without calling it a loss.
cells.verb: Letting go on purpose when something is finished
cells.place: At the threshold where a work is complete and the next step begins

cells.tense: The ending will be hurried, because staying until it is finished feels like it might never arrive.
cells.act: do the plain version first, before the plans
cells.ask: You'd rather walk off before it finishes. Do the plain, unglamorous version instead — the smallest complete form. No upgrade, no announcement, no exit speech. The belated finish may sting more than bolting would have.
cells.core:
When something nears its end, you can release it a beat early — call it over before it has actually ended, skip the last turn because the finish already feels late. You leave first, so nothing gets to leave you. What's skipped is the piece that would have made the closing clean.

Take the plain ending before you improvise a bigger one. Finish the thing at the size it actually is, not at the size your story about it demands. Let it be small and complete rather than large and abandoned. The person who watches doesn't need the drama, and neither do you.
cells.sheetLine: You end it early so the ending can't reach you.
cells.verb: Letting go on purpose when something is finished

cells.tense: The grip stays closed on a thing that finished, and the arm holding it has gone sore.
cells.act: bear the next hour of it without deciding anything
cells.ask: Your hand keeps ahold of a weight without you deciding to. Stay through one ordinary hour of it and settle nothing. Don't force the drop, don't plan it. Nobody says the hand must open — only notice you're still holding on.
cells.core:
The ending came, and the hands are still closed around something that already stopped being yours to carry. What was going to be set down stayed held, and now that is the work — kept so steadily the shoulders have forgotten they could drop. Releasing isn't refused here — it has simply dropped out of the available moves.

Don't sit down to practice release. Stand through the next hour without settling one thing about it. The following work will begin when it begins, and until then, holding at the true size is enough. That tightness is not a verdict on who you are. It's a grip that hasn't heard the news yet.

cells.tense: You have already put it down, and you still tell the story as if you were carrying it.
cells.act: keep showing up to it without forcing a result
cells.ask: One story you tell about a hard stretch has an ending you actually reached, not the one you repeat. Go back to that finished thing, name what changed, once, and skip the bow after.
cells.core:
When you finish with something and truly leave it finished, you don't turn back to check its weight. The hands are empty, and you walk toward what's next without a backward narration. Done means done, and you can feel that the way you feel a room when the noise stops.

In one story you tell about a hard season, the ending you actually reached is already there — but you file it under what happened to you, or under the fight, or under nothing at all. Go back to that ending with nothing added. Sit with one hard thing you finished, name what changed, plain, once. The plainest version is the true one.
cells.sheetLine: You already let it go. The telling hasn't caught up.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that I can see what in the person's history made letting go hard — that detail never crossed my table, so the Too Little cell names the paralysis only where it is visible. The reader could fairly say the body keeps no grip and the story is being told by the mind; I have described the mechanism only in moments I could be shown, not its causes. The ask survives being wrong: even if none of it lands, the person is left holding one small tendered thing, not a verdict. The sentence that serves me rather than them is 'you get to put something down' — a phrase built to sound like relief; I left it out because relief is not in the record, and only the conditions for release are.
